Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 6 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Coming of Age and Conflicting Perspectives

Lesson Focus

Primary Standard: MLA.CW.FIC.07 — develop coming-of-age change through conflicting perspectives, consequential choices, and qualified insight.

What You Will Learn

  • Distinguish maturation from simply getting older.
  • Build conflict between defensible perspectives rather than a correct person and a foolish one.
  • Trace a protagonist’s belief, challenge, choice, cost, and revised understanding.
  • Use viewpoint limits and counterevidence to avoid simplistic lessons.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 6 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task

Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.

TermMeaningExample
coming-of-age narrativeA story centered on a significant change in maturity, identity, responsibility, or understanding.The coming-of-age narrative follows a teenager learning to accept responsibility.
maturationGrowth in judgment or responsibility produced through experience and reflection.Admitting the harm he caused marks the character’s maturation.
worldviewA person’s organized assumptions about how people and society work.Experience changes her worldview about fairness and power.
perspectiveA position shaped by knowledge, experience, values, and interests.The narrator’s perspective shifts after hearing the opposing account.
conflicting perspectivesDifferent interpretations or priorities that cannot all be satisfied at once.The siblings’ conflicting perspectives create tension about leaving home.
defensible positionA viewpoint supported by understandable evidence or values, even if imperfect.The character’s actions and evidence support a defensible position about his growth.
counterevidenceEvidence that challenges or limits an initial belief.His final selfish decision serves as counterevidence to the claim that he has fully changed.
recognitionA moment when a character understands something previously missed or resisted.The protagonist’s recognition that fear guided her choices begins the climax.
agencyA character’s capacity to make meaningful choices and affect outcomes.Choosing to speak publicly demonstrates agency.
costly choiceA decision that requires a real sacrifice, risk, or loss.Returning the stolen money is a costly choice because it risks punishment.
internal conflictStruggle among competing beliefs, desires, loyalties, or fears within a character.The desire for approval conflicts with personal values, creating internal conflict.
earned changeA believable transformation prepared by pressure, evidence, choice, and consequence.The final decision grows from earlier failures, making the change feel earned.

Vocabulary Application — Try It

Use each sentence’s context to place the correct term. Choose Check, study the result, and retry any missed item. This is ungraded practice.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 6 | Page 3 of 6

Direct Teaching: Building Earned Growth

Seven-Step Growth Arc

  1. State the protagonist’s initial belief.
  2. Show why that belief once made sense.
  3. Introduce a defensible conflicting perspective.
  4. Present counterevidence the protagonist cannot easily dismiss.
  5. Force a costly choice before full certainty is available.
  6. Show consequence rather than instant wisdom.
  7. End with revised behavior that demonstrates qualified change.

Visual Growth Arc

INITIAL BELIEFCHALLENGECOUNTEREVIDENCECOSTLY CHOICEREVISED ACTION
Certainty → Friction → Complexity → Agency → Earned change
Learning routes: graph confidence before and after each beat; role-read both perspectives aloud; or sort evidence cards beneath each worldview.

Pause and Choose: Build a Defensible Conflict

A teenager wants to leave the family business, while an aunt asks for time to train a younger cousin. Which version gives both perspectives credible values and evidence?

A. “The teenager values freedom, while the selfish aunt refuses to accept change.”
Not the best choice. Labeling the aunt selfish makes one side obviously wrong and prevents evidence from genuinely challenging the protagonist’s belief.
B. “The teenager values independence after years of work; the aunt values a responsible transition because the cousin’s training is incomplete.”
✓ Correct—both positions can withstand scrutiny. Each perspective has a legitimate value and evidence, so the protagonist must weigh competing obligations rather than defeat a caricature.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Perspective Matrix

QuestionPerspective APerspective B
What does each value?name valuename value
What evidence is available?known factsknown facts
What is each missing?blind spotblind spot
What would change the view?thresholdthreshold

Avoid False Maturity

Growth is not automatic obedience, perfect certainty, or abandoning youth. A character may mature by questioning an adult, setting a boundary, accepting responsibility, admitting uncertainty, or revising a judgment.

Pause and Choose: Show Earned Growth

Which ending demonstrates qualified maturation through costly action instead of instant wisdom or obedience?

A. “After the aunt’s speech, the teenager realized adults were always right and abandoned the plan to leave.”
Not the best choice. One speech produces total reversal, removes the character’s original valid goal, and equates maturity with obedience.
B. “The teenager proposes six weeks of training, postponing departure while keeping a firm final date and asking the cousin to help design the transition.”
✓ Correct—the revised behavior shows agency and cost. Evidence reshapes the plan without erasing independence. The character accepts temporary responsibility and creates a boundary that protects the long-term goal.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Common Failures

  • Making the opposing perspective obviously foolish.
  • Using one speech to transform the protagonist instantly.
  • Confusing trauma with automatic growth.
  • Removing agency by having adults solve the conflict.
  • Ending with explanation instead of changed behavior.

Pause and Try — Build an Earned Turning Point

Situation: A teenager wants to leave the family business immediately. An aunt argues that the teenager should stay until a younger cousin is trained. Both perspectives have credible evidence.

Your turn: State the teenager’s initial belief, the aunt’s defensible position, one piece of counterevidence, and a costly choice that could show maturation.

Check your thinking with the teacher model

The teenager initially believes that leaving now is the only way to claim an independent life. The aunt argues that sudden departure would place an unfair burden on the cousin. The cousin’s admission that the training is incomplete becomes counterevidence.

A mature choice might be a six-week transition plan. It costs the teenager immediate freedom, but it protects the cousin while preserving the long-term goal. The change is earned because evidence reshapes—rather than erases—the original perspective.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 6 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Earned-Change Models

Example 1 — Revise Obedience Into Judgment

Weak: A teen matures by accepting that her coach is always right.

  1. Initial belief: asking for rest shows weakness.
  2. Coach’s defensible view: consistency builds trust.
  3. Counterevidence: a teammate hides an injury.
  4. Choice: the protagonist reports the injury and risks her position.
  5. Consequence: teammate receives care; trust with coach is strained.
  6. Earned change: she distinguishes commitment from silence.

Example 2 — Two Defensible Perspectives

A student wants to publish a family history; an aunt wants to keep one painful event private.

  1. Student values preservation and accuracy.
  2. Aunt values consent and protection.
  3. Both possess different evidence.
  4. Turn: another relative requests inclusion.
  5. Choice: publish a documented gap rather than the private account.
  6. Growth: the student learns that accuracy includes naming limits.

Example 3 — Change Through Action

A protagonist who mocks a neighbor’s emergency supplies faces a blackout.

  1. Do not end with “He learned preparation mattered.”
  2. Counterevidence: supplies help, but hoarding excludes others.
  3. Choice: he organizes shared distribution rather than copying the neighbor.
  4. Cost: he gives up his own guaranteed portion.
  5. Revised action shows a qualified insight about preparation and community.
  6. Ending preserves disagreement over how much is enough.

Model Grid

ModelFalse versionEarned version
Athleteobedienceresponsible dissent
Historytotal disclosureaccuracy with consent
Blackoutcopy an adultnew communal response

Choose A or B — Which Ending Shows Earned Change?

Conflict: A teenager wants independence but learns that leaving immediately would harm a younger cousin.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which ending shows earned change while preserving the conflict between independence and responsibility?

A. The teenager stays because an adult orders it, proving that maturity means obedience.
Weaker response. The character becomes passive, and the change is not supported through recognition, agency, and consequence.
B. The teenager delays leaving, arranges safe care for the cousin, and accepts the cost of missing the first opportunity while preserving a later path to independence.
Stronger response. The character makes a costly choice that integrates both perspectives, showing that independence can include responsibility rather than simply surrendering it.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Your Turn — Revise the action, then check the reasoning

A strong revision should make the character choose, sacrifice something meaningful, and act on a more complex understanding. The final action—not a narrator’s explanation—should prove the maturation.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 3 | Lesson 6 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Coming of Age and Conflicting Perspectives

Purpose

Reveal growth by placing a character between competing, believable perspectives.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Your work should show deliberate choices, not just completion.

Source for Your Work

Sixteen-year-old Dani wants to accept an apprenticeship in another city. Dani’s older sibling believes leaving means abandoning the family during a difficult year.

1. Plan Before You Draft

DecisionYour Plan
Character goal and obstacleWrite one clear sentence.
Key turning pointState the choice or discovery.
Meaning readers should inferName the idea without writing a moral.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach would produce stronger creative writing? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Make Dani correct and the sibling selfish so the conflict is easy to resolve.
B. Give both characters valid concerns, then let Dani’s response show a more mature understanding of freedom and responsibility.

3. Apply the Lesson

Draft a 350–450 word scene in which Dani and the sibling confront the decision. Use dialogue, internal thought, and one meaningful action to show both perspectives and a step in Dani’s growth.

4. Revise with Purpose

Revise one exchange so each speaker’s reasoning is understandable while their voices remain distinct.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your creative work applies the lesson skill and uses the source provided.
  • Your explanation names a specific choice and its effect.
  • Your revision improves meaning or craft, not only spelling.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Coming of Age and Conflicting Perspectives

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original writing, and explain your craft decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: The Apprenticeship Letter

Sana held the acceptance letter behind her back. The coastal workshop had chosen only four apprentices, and she was one of them. Her grandfather studied the fishing nets piled beside the door. “Your hands are needed here,” he said. Sana looked at the patched roof, then at the train schedule tucked inside the envelope. “If I never learn to build stronger boats,” she answered, “our work stays exactly as fragile as it is now.”

A coming-of-age arc shows a young person gaining maturity through difficult choices. Conflicting perspectives are differing interpretations shaped by each person’s values, experience, and needs.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Explain the values and concerns behind Sana’s perspective and her grandfather’s perspective. Use evidence for both.
  2. What choice could reveal Sana’s growth without making either character simply right or wrong?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which plan creates a more complex coming-of-age conflict?

A. Make the grandfather selfish and unreasonable so readers automatically support Sana.
B. Give both characters valid concerns, then show Sana making a choice that accepts responsibility for its consequences.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Write a 450–600 word coming-of-age scene with two credible perspectives.

  1. Opening: Establish the young character’s goal, the relationship, and what is at stake.
  2. Development: Use dialogue and action to reveal the reasoning behind both perspectives.
  3. Turning point: Require the young character to make a difficult choice and accept a cost.
  4. Resolution: Show a consequence that demonstrates growth without erasing the conflict.

Add a 3–4 sentence reflection explaining how the turning point shows maturity.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the reader should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Find one place where a perspective seems flat or unfair. Add a detail that makes the character’s reasoning more credible without resolving the disagreement.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise the organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the writing becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The writing follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
